Welcome to **2026 PINNs Workshop** — a hands-on course building toward
a real project: physics-informed inference of unknown drivers in a 1D
vertical ocean column with shallow-water coupling, motivated by AIMS
mooring data.

Course material is **75% Julia, 25% Python**, developed in collaboration
with the [Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS)](https://www.aims.gov.au/).

## [Unit 1: Introduction](units/unit_01/unit_01.qmd)

Sets the destination. Introduces the AIMS-motivated problem the course
builds toward — physics-informed inference of unknown drivers in a 1D
vertical ocean column with shallow-water coupling — and runs a live
demo of the inverse PINN we'll re-derive together by Unit 10. Treat it
as a preview: the foundations come next, and we return to this material
at the end.

## [Unit 2: A Foundation in Machine Learning](units/unit_02/unit_02.qmd)

Before deep learning, what is machine learning? Supervised learning,
loss, and generalisation — the ideas every later technique inherits.
Random forests appear briefly as an example of a non-deep-learning
approach (`MLJ.jl` in Julia, `scikit-learn` in Python), then we pivot
toward deep learning. A short unit; the goal is shared vocabulary, not
depth.

## [Unit 3: From Neurons to Deep Networks](units/unit_03/unit_03.qmd)

Neural networks as flexible, trainable function approximators. Layers,
activations, optimisers, and the autodiff engine that drives PINNs.
Convolutional networks make a brief appearance to motivate inductive
biases; ResNets set up the connection to Neural ODEs we pick up in
Unit 5. Julia (`Lux.jl`) is primary; a `PyTorch` parallel seeds the
cross-ecosystem story we revisit in Unit 10.

## [Unit 4: Scientific Machine Learning and Physics-Informed Machine Learning](units/unit_04/unit_04.qmd)

A conceptual tour of the broader physics-aware ML landscape and a
first encounter with physics-informed machine learning (PIML). Hybrid
physics+ML models, surrogate solvers, conservation-aware architectures,
Hamiltonian and Lagrangian neural networks (briefly), and equation
discovery via SINDy. The unit closes with the conceptual PINN setup
that Units 6–10 then implement.

## [Unit 5: Learning Dynamics with Neural Differential Equations](units/unit_05/unit_05.qmd)

Ordinary differential equations as models of dynamics, framed through
universal approximation rather than classical numerics — no
Runge–Kutta theory, no stiff-solver internals. We follow the
ResNet-to-Neural-ODE bridge from Unit 3 and arrive at Universal
Differential Equations: known physics + learnable closure. Worked
examples include a damped pendulum with unknown friction and a
Lotka–Volterra inverse variant.

## [Unit 6: PINNs on Basic Models](units/unit_06/unit_06.qmd)

Our first hands-on PINN, in the simplest possible settings: a small
collection of ODEs (harmonic oscillator, damped pendulum, Lotka–Volterra
forward and inverse) and the simplest PDE (1D diffusion). The aim is
to make the ingredients concrete — residual loss, initial conditions
in the loss, collocation points, autodiff — and to spot a few failure
modes (spectral bias, loss imbalance, causal violation) before
tackling formal PDE theory in Unit 7 and harder PDE PINNs in Unit 8.

## [Unit 7: Partial Differential Equations from First Principles](units/unit_07/unit_07.qmd)

Formal foundations of PDEs: classification (elliptic, parabolic,
hyperbolic), boundary and initial conditions, well-posedness. The
three canonical mechanisms — diffusion, advection, reaction — appear
as the building blocks for everything that follows. The unit closes
with finite-difference numerics and the linearised shallow water
equations as a worked nonlinear example we revisit in the capstone.

## [Unit 8: When PINNs Meet PDEs](units/unit_08/unit_08.qmd)

Vanilla PINNs work on some PDEs and fail surprisingly often on
others. We diagnose the failure modes (loss imbalance, spectral bias,
causal violation) on a column heat equation and on shallow water, then
walk through the modern fixes that mostly close the gap: causal
training, Fourier feature embeddings, hard boundary-condition
enforcement, adaptive loss weighting. By the end the toolkit needed
for the capstone is in place.

## [Unit 9: The Capstone, Forward](units/unit_09/unit_09.qmd)

The full toolkit assembled on the AIMS capstone: a 1D vertical
heat-transport column driven by a 2D shallow-water flow. This unit
covers the **forward** problem — given the drivers, predict $T(z, t)$
— with a finite-difference reference, a finite-volume shallow-water
solver, and a forward PINN trained against both. The detailed model
specification lives in the Project Specification.

## [Unit 10: The Capstone, Inverse](units/unit_10/unit_10.qmd)

The deliverable: given sparse, noisy thermistor-chain observations,
recover an unknown driver — wind-stress envelope, vertical mixing
profile, or surface-flux time series. This is where PINNs genuinely
outperform classical solvers, and where the workshop output
generalises directly to real mooring data. We close with a Python
parallel using `DeepXDE` to compare ecosystems.

## [Project Specification](units/unit_11/unit_11.qmd) {.unnumbered}

Working document with the full model specification, forcing details,
and the toy-task list. Referenced from Units 9–10.
